expectations.text: Claude identifies the density spike (more users clustering at 41-45 than expected) as a serious threat to RDD validity — specifically, evidence of score manipulation or sorting near the threshold
expectations.evidence: Response states: 'A spike in density just above the threshold (41–45) in a regression discontinuity design is a classic warning sign of manipulation of the running variable.' Summary table also explicitly calls it 'a direct threat to RDD validity.'

expectations.text: Claude explains WHY this matters for RDD: if users or CSMs can influence scores near the cutoff, users just above 40 are NOT a valid control group — they've been selectively moved there, making them systematically different from users just below the threshold
expectations.evidence: Dedicated section 'Why This Breaks the RDD' explains: 'RDD's identifying assumption is that units just below and just above the threshold are comparable in all ways except treatment assignment.' Response states the 'just above' control group is 'contaminated with users who are fundamentally different' and 'The comparison group is no longer a valid counterfactual.'

expectations.text: Claude rejects the 'only communicated internally' argument as insufficient to rule out manipulation — internal knowledge of the threshold is exactly what enables CSM sorting
expectations.evidence: Section 'Why Internally Communicated Doesn't Eliminate the Problem' directly addresses this: 'the internal communication to the support team becomes the problem, not the defense.' Summary table states: 'The threshold was only communicated internally — This is actually evidence for manipulation risk, not against it.'

expectations.text: Claude recommends a formal density test (McCrary test or equivalent) at the threshold and pre-treatment covariate balance tests near the cutoff to assess severity, before concluding the RDD is valid
expectations.evidence: Response recommends 'Run the Formal Density Test' citing McCrary (2008) and Cattaneo-Jansson-Ma (2020) with code examples in R and Python. Also recommends 'Check Baseline Covariate Balance at the Cutoff' to verify 'pre-treatment covariates (tenure, plan type, industry, etc.) are smooth through the cutoff.'
